arXiv:2404.18463v1 [math.NA] 29 Apr 2024

Efficient bound preserving and asymptotic preserving semi-implicit schemes for the fast reaction–diffusion system

Yu Zhao ††thanks: Corresponding author.††thanks: School of Mathematics, Statistics and Mechanics, Beijing University of Technology, Beijing, 100124, P.R.China.
E-mail: y.zhao@bjut.edu.cn    Zhennan Zhou ††thanks: Institute for Theoretical Sciences, Westlake University, Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, 310030, P.R.China.
E-mail: zhouzhennan@westlake.edu.cn
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We consider a special type of fast reaction–diffusion systems in which the coefficients of the reaction terms of the two substances are much larger than those of the diffusion terms while the diffusive motion to the substrate is negligible. Specifically speaking, the rate constants of the reaction terms are O⁡(1/ϵ)O(1/\epsilon) while the diffusion coefficients are O⁡(1)O(1) where the parameter ϵ\epsilon is small. When the rate constants of the reaction terms become highly large, i.e. ϵ\epsilon tends to 0, the singular limit behavior of such a fast reaction–diffusion system is inscribed by the Stefan problem with latent heat, which brings great challenges in numerical simulations. In this paper, we adopt a semi-implicit scheme, which is first-order accurate in time and can accurately approximate the interface propagation even when the reaction becomes extremely fast, that is to say, the parameter ϵ\epsilon is sufficiently small. The scheme satisfies the positivity, bound preserving properties and has L2L^{2} stability and the linearized stability results of the system. For better performance on numerical simulations, we then construct a semi-implicit Runge–Kutta scheme which is second-order accurate in time. Numerous numerical tests are carried out to demonstrate the properties, such as the order of accuracy, positivity and bound preserving, the capturing of the sharp interface with various ϵ\epsilon and to simulate the dynamics of the substances and the substrate, and to explore the heat transfer process, such as solid melting or liquid solidification in two dimensions.

Keywords. Fast reaction, Stefan problem, multi-scale time scales, semi-implicit method.

AMS subject classification. 35Q92, 65M06, 65M12, 92E20.

1 Introduction

The reaction–diffusion equations are a class of partial differential equations that describe the dynamics of a system in which some quantity, such as the concentration of a chemical, diffuses through space while undergoing some kind of reaction including a chemical reaction. Such equations have a wide range of promising applications to describe phenomena arising from natural and social sciences, such as the population dynamics [17], the chemical reactions [16, 31], the neuronal responses [13, 15] and the enterprise competition [33]. The fast reaction–diffusion system is a special case of reaction–diffusion systems in which the strength of the reaction term of chemical substances is much greater than that of the diffusion term. It has been widely applied to describe cancer, wound healing, and the regeneration of tissues and bones, and has aroused great research interest in the fields of medicine and biology [25]. For instance, as for the penetration of radiolabeling antibodies into tumor tissues, the penetration rate of antibodies is very slow due to their large size, while antibodies attach to antigens and react quickly, so the whole process can be described by a fast reaction–diffusion system [12].

In this work, we shall be concerned with a special type of fast reaction–diffusion systems, in which there are two reactants and one substrate. In such systems, the two reactants’ dynamics in concentration are determined by both the regular diffusion and fast reactions, while the evolution of the substrate’s concentration is governed only by its fast reaction. The rate constants of the reactions are O⁡(1/ϵ)O(1/\epsilon) and the diffusion coefficients are O⁡(1)O(1) where the parameter ϵ\epsilon is sufficiently small. Specifically, we consider the following semi-linear equations:

∂tuϵ−d1​Δ​uϵ\displaystyle\partial_{t}u_{\epsilon}-d_{1}\Delta u_{\epsilon} =−1ϵ​uϵ​[vϵ+λ⁡(1−pϵ)],x∈ℝd,t>0,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}u_{\epsilon}\left[v_{\epsilon}+\lambda\left(1-p_{\epsilon}\right)\right],~~x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},~~t>0, (1)
∂tvϵ−d2​Δ​vϵ\displaystyle\partial_{t}v_{\epsilon}-d_{2}\Delta v_{\epsilon} =−1ϵ​vϵ​(uϵ+λ​pϵ),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}v_{\epsilon}\left(u_{\epsilon}+\lambda p_{\epsilon}\right), (2)
∂tpϵ\displaystyle\partial_{t}p_{\epsilon} =1ϵ​[(1−pϵ)​uϵ−vϵ​pϵ],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left[\left(1-p_{\epsilon}\right)u_{\epsilon}-v_{\epsilon}p_{\epsilon}\right], (3)

where uϵ=uϵ​(x,t)u_{\epsilon}=u_{\epsilon}(x,t) and vϵ=vϵ​(x,t)v_{\epsilon}=v_{\epsilon}(x,t) represent the concentrations of the two reactants and pϵ=pϵ​(x,t)p_{\epsilon}=p_{\epsilon}(x,t) represents the concentration of the substrate with x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} indicating the location and t>0t>0 indicating the time [11, 28]. λ>0\lambda>0 is a constant, and d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0 are the diffusion coefficients of the two reactants. The initial condition of the equations (1)-(3) is

uϵ​(x,0)=uϵ0​(x),vϵ​(x,0)=vϵ0​(x),pϵ​(x,0)=pϵ0​(x),\displaystyle u_{\epsilon}(x,0)=u_{\epsilon}^{0}(x),\quad v_{\epsilon}(x,0)=v_{\epsilon}^{0}(x),\quad p_{\epsilon}(x,0)=p_{\epsilon}^{0}(x), (4)

where uϵ0​(x),vϵ0​(x)u_{\epsilon}^{0}(x),v_{\epsilon}^{0}(x) and pϵ0​(x)p_{\epsilon}^{0}(x) are given.

Following [28], there are several main properties for the fast reaction–diffusion system (1)-(4): non-negativity, upper bound preserving and limit behavior describing.

    Bound preserving.
    With the non-negative initial data satisfying uniform upper bounds in ϵ\epsilon, i.e.

    The limit behavior of the system (1)-(4) is described by the Stefan problem.
    Under the assumption (5), one expects to find the strong limits u=u⁡(x,t)≥0,v=v⁡(x,t)≥0u=u(x,t)\geq 0,v=v(x,t)\geq 0 and 0≤p=p⁡(x,t)≤10\leq p=p(x,t)\leq 1 of the solutions uϵ,vϵu_{\epsilon},v_{\epsilon} and pϵp_{\epsilon} as ϵ\epsilon tends to 00 in the system (1)-(4). This implies that the limits u,vu,v and pp satisfy

    v=0,p=1,if ​u>0,u=0,p=0,if ​v>0,p∈[0,1],if ​u=v=0.\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{ll}v=0,~~p=1,&\text{if~~}u>0,\\ u=0,~~p=0,&\text{if~~}v>0,\\ p\in[0,1],&\text{if~~}u=v=0.\end{array}

    Let wϵ=uϵ−vϵ+λ​pϵw_{\epsilon}=u_{\epsilon}-v_{\epsilon}+\lambda p_{\epsilon} and w=u−v+λ​pw=u-v+\lambda p, then the limit ww of wϵw_{\epsilon} solves the problem

    ∂tw−Δ​B​(w)=0,x∈ℝn,t>0,\displaystyle\partial_{t}w-\Delta B(w)=0,~~x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},~~t>0, (9)

    where B⁡(⋅)B(\cdot) is a nonlinear diffusion function defined by

    B⁡(w):={d2​w,if ​w<0,0,if ​0≤w≤λ,d1​(w−λ),if ​w>λ.\displaystyle B(w):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}d_{2}w,&\text{if~~}w<0,\\ 0,&\text{if~~}0\leq w\leq\lambda,\\ d_{1}(w-\lambda),&\text{if~~}w>\lambda.\end{array}\right.

    The equation (9) is called the Stefan problem with λ\lambda representing the latent heat. ww in the Stefan problem (9) is called the enthalpy function of a substance, a thermodynamic state function that describes the total energy content of a system at a constant pressure, and B⁡(w)B(w) is referred to as the temperature of the substance. The expression (9) describes the relationship between the temperature and enthalpy of the substance.

As the limit of the fast reaction–diffusion system (1)-(4) when ϵ\epsilon tends to 0, the Stefan problem portrays the heat transfer process in the material undergoing a phase change. In the heat transfer process, the movement velocity of the interface between different phases of the substance is inscribed by the Stefan condition [26, 10]. The Stefan problem is named after the Austrian physicist Josef Stefan, who first proposed the problem in the 19th century [29]. And such a problem has wild applications in various fields, such as materials science, thermodynamics, and geophysics. It is commonly used to study the solidification and melting of metals, the freezing and thawing of soil, and the behavior of sea ice. Nowadays the Stefan problem has received great attentions in the ice accumulation problem on an aircraft and inspired by this, an enthalpy-based modeling framework to quantify uncertainty in Stefan problems with an injection boundary is developed in [34].

In terms of numerics, many efforts have been devoted to solving general reaction–diffusion equations and the Stefan problem respectively. With respect to a reaction–diffusion equation, various numerical methods have been developed to approximate the solutions. Among them, the time-stepping methods mainly include explicit schemes, semi-implicit schemes [23], fully implicit schemes [24], explicit-implicit schemes [8, 20, 14, 32] and exponential time difference schemes [19, 6, 18], etc. Regarding the numerical discretization in space, the main focus is on the finite difference method, the finite element method [23], and the non-standard finite difference method [1, 27], etc. With respect to the Stefan problem, it is a challenging problem to solve it either analytically or numerically due to the moving interface, singularities and nonlinearities. Wherein accurately capturing the movement of the sharp interface between different phases has been the focus and main difficulty. The study of numerical methods for approximating the solution and capturing the sharp interface has attracted extensive attention from many researchers. Depending on the different ways of tracking the sharp interface, numerical simulation methods of the Stefan problem are broadly categorized into two directions. One is to discretize the moving boundary problem directly based on the interface’s movement velocity inscribed by the Stefan condition, such as fixed-grid finite difference methods [21, 4] and moving-grid finite difference methods [21, 2]. The other approach is to capture the interface’s movement process implicitly by or based on enthalpy methods [4, 7, 2, 9, 22, 30, 5, 34].

It is a challenging problem to find a class of efficient numerical methods that can simulate both such a fast reaction–diffusion system (1)-(4) and its limit behavior which is described by the Stefan problem (9) as ϵ\epsilon tends to 0 in spite of the existing works in either direction. To be specific, the difficulty lies in several factors, including non-negativity, upper-bound preserving, stiffness, nonlinearity, parameter sensitivity, asymptotic preserving, etc. Therefore we aim to develop a class of efficient schemes for this type of fast reaction–diffusion system, which can not only overcome the stiffness and nonlinearity and have the non-negativity preserving and bound preserving properties on the numerical side based on the physical meaning and analytical properties of the continuum model, but also capture the limit behavior of the Stefan problem when ϵ\epsilon in the numerical scheme tends to 0.

In this work, we will adopt a semi-implicit scheme, that is of first-order accuracy in time. Such a scheme not only satisfies the non-negativity and upper-bound preserving properties at the discrete level, but also has the stability results. And it can accurately capture the interface propagation even with extremely fast reactions. We will also construct a semi-implicit Runge–Kutta scheme which is second-order accurate in time following the methodology presented in [3]. In addition, we perform numerical simulations of concentrations of the substances in chemical reactions, predictions of enthalpy function’s behaviors in the Stefan problem and capture of sharp interfaces, thus showing strong promise for practical simulations of realistic scientific problems and providing much understanding of the nature of the mathematics behind the problem of aircraft ice accumulation.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we first consider the semi-implicit treatment to the fast reaction–diffusion system (1)-(4) which is of first-order accuracy in time, and prove that such a semi-discrete semi-implicit scheme satisfies the non-negativity preserving, bound preserving properties. Moreover, L2L^{2} stability results of our scheme and the stability results of the corresponding scheme to the linearized system of (1)-(4) are given. Then error estimates of the scheme about the reactivity coefficients are provided. At last, we construct a fully-discrete semi-implicit finite difference scheme. A semi-implicit Runge–Kutta scheme which is second-order accurate in time is outlined in section 3. In section 4 we verify the properties of our numerical methods with numerous test examples, such as numerical accuracy, non-negativity and bound preserving, and the capturing of the sharp interface with various ϵ\epsilon. Additionally, specified numerical tests are carried out with care to make simulations of the dynamics of the substances and substrate in chemical reactions and to demonstrate the processes of melting or solidification. Some concluding remarks are made in section 5.

2 Semi-implicit scheme and analysis

In this section, to avoid the use of nonlinear solvers and improve the stability, we apply a semi-implicit strategy on the fast reaction–diffusion system (1)-(4) and propose the semi-implicit numerical schemes with the first-order convergence in time. And the numerical analysis of our scheme is presented in the following part.

2.1 Semi-implicit treatment

To avoid solving nonlinear equations required by a fully implicit scheme, we focus on the semi-implicit strategy. When discretizing the equations (1)-(3) in time, to improve the stability, we treat the diffusion terms in equations (1)-(2) implicitly. Then for the sake of computational simplicity and decoupling of solutions, uu in equation (1), vv in equation (2) and pp in equation (3) are treated implicitly while the latest values are used for the other variables in each equation. Hence when discretizing the equations (1)-(3) in time, we adopt the following semi-implicit treatment to obtain the semi-discrete scheme

pn+1−pnτ\displaystyle\frac{p^{n+1}-p^{n}}{\tau} =1ϵ​[(1−pn+1)​un−vn​pn+1],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left[\left(1-p^{n+1}\right)u^{n}-v^{n}p^{n+1}\right], (13)
un+1−unτ−d1​Δ​un+1\displaystyle\frac{u^{n+1}-u^{n}}{\tau}-d_{1}\Delta u^{n+1} =−1ϵ​un+1​[vn+λ⁡(1−pn+1)],\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}u^{n+1}\left[v^{n}+\lambda\left(1-p^{n+1}\right)\right], (14)
vn+1−vnτ−d2​Δ​vn+1\displaystyle\frac{v^{n+1}-v^{n}}{\tau}-d_{2}\Delta v^{n+1} =−1ϵ​vn+1​(un+1+λ​pn+1),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}v^{n+1}\left(u^{n+1}+\lambda p^{n+1}\right), (15)

where un,vn,pnu^{n},v^{n},p^{n} are the approximation solutions to equations (1)-(3) at t=tn:=n​τt=t_{n}:=n\tau with τ>0\tau>0 being the temporal size and n=0,1,⋯n=0,1,\cdots. Here in order to simplify the expression of the formulas, we drop the index ϵ\epsilon, and the same applies in the rest of the paper. We would like to highlight that such a semi-implicit treatment results in many numerical advantages, and we start by listing some desired properties of the semi-discrete scheme (13)-(15) in the following.

If the condition (5) holds for the initial data, the semi-discrete scheme (13)-(15) satisfies the non-negativity and upper-bound preserving properties.

Lemma 2.1 and Lemma 2.2 tell us that the semi-discrete semi-implicit scheme (13)-(15) is not only solved without a nonlinear solver, but also maintains the properties of the solutions of the fast reaction–diffusion system (1)-(4), including the non-negativity, upper-bound preserving properties and the L2L^{2} stability results. When considering the fully discrete scheme, the effect of the boundary conditions will be studied as well.

Note that the estimate above is near the spatial homogeneous limiting solution (17). Next, we investigate the limiting behavior involving dynamical phase transition. Following the fact that the limit behavior of the system (1)-(4) is described by the Stefan problem (9) as ϵ\epsilon tends to 0, we give the residual error estimates of the scheme (13)-(15) about the reactivity coefficients.

Let wn=un−vn+λ​pnw^{n}=u^{n}-v^{n}+\lambda p^{n}, then the semi-discrete semi-implicit scheme (13)-(15) leads that

wn+1−wnτ−d1​Δ​un+1+d2​Δ​vn+1=Rn+1,\displaystyle\frac{w^{n+1}-w^{n}}{\tau}-d_{1}\Delta u^{n+1}+d_{2}\Delta v^{n+1}=R^{n+1},

where the residual error

Rn+1=−1ϵ​un+1​[vn+λ⁡(1−pn+1)]+1ϵ​vn+1​(un+1+λ​pn+1)+λϵ​[(1−pn+1)​un−vn​pn+1].\displaystyle R^{n+1}=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}u^{n+1}\left[v^{n}+\lambda\left(1-p^{n+1}\right)\right]+\frac{1}{\epsilon}v^{n+1}(u^{n+1}+\lambda p^{n+1})+\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon}\left[\left(1-p^{n+1}\right)u^{n}-v^{n}p^{n+1}\right].

We mention that if the condition (5) holds for the initial data, the semi-discrete solution wn=un−vn+λ​pnw^{n}=u^{n}-v^{n}+\lambda p^{n} is a good approximation to the solution of the Stefan problem (9) as long as ϵ\epsilon tends to 0 and τ\tau is small enough.

In fact, assume that ϵ\epsilon tends to 0 and the condition (5) holds, then for n=1,2,⋯n=1,2,\cdots, we consider the expansion expressions

un=∑k=0∞ukn​ϵk,vn=∑k=0∞vkn​ϵk,pn=∑k=0∞pkn​ϵk.\displaystyle u^{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}u^{n}_{k}\epsilon^{k},\quad v^{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}v^{n}_{k}\epsilon^{k},\quad p^{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}p^{n}_{k}\epsilon^{k}. (48)

On one hand, plugging the expressions (48) into the residual error Rn+1R^{n+1}, one gets Rn+1=∑k=−1∞Rkn+1​O​(ϵk)R^{n+1}=\sum_{k=-1}^{\infty}R_{k}^{n+1}O(\epsilon^{k}), where

R−1n+1=−u0n+1​[v0n+λ⁡(1−p0n+1)]+v0n+1​(u0n+1+λ​p0n+1)+λ⁡[(1−p0n+1)​u0n−v0n​p0n+1],R_{-1}^{n+1}=-u_{0}^{n+1}\left[v_{0}^{n}+\lambda\left(1-p_{0}^{n+1}\right)\right]+v_{0}^{n+1}(u_{0}^{n+1}+\lambda p_{0}^{n+1})+\lambda\left[\left(1-p_{0}^{n+1}\right)u_{0}^{n}-v_{0}^{n}p_{0}^{n+1}\right],

and

R0n+1=∑i+j=1(−uin+1​vjn+λ​uin+1​pjn+1+uin+1​vjn+1+λ​vin+1​pjn+1−λ​uin​pjn+1−λ​vin​pjn+1)−λ​u1n+1+λ​u1n.R_{0}^{n+1}=\sum_{i+j=1}\left(-u_{i}^{n+1}v_{j}^{n}+\lambda u_{i}^{n+1}p_{j}^{n+1}+u_{i}^{n+1}v_{j}^{n+1}+\lambda v_{i}^{n+1}p_{j}^{n+1}-\lambda u_{i}^{n}p_{j}^{n+1}-\lambda v_{i}^{n}p_{j}^{n+1}\right)-\lambda u_{1}^{n+1}+\lambda u_{1}^{n}.

On the other hand, plugging the expressions (48) into the semi-discrete scheme (13)-(15) and comparing O⁡(ϵ−1)O({\epsilon}^{-1}) term in the left and right sides of the scheme, we obtain

0\displaystyle 0 =(1−p0n+1)​u0n−v0n​p0n+1,\displaystyle=\left(1-p_{0}^{n+1}\right)u_{0}^{n}-v_{0}^{n}p_{0}^{n+1},
0\displaystyle 0 =u0n+1​[v0n+λ⁡(1−p0n+1)],\displaystyle=u_{0}^{n+1}\left[v_{0}^{n}+\lambda\left(1-p_{0}^{n+1}\right)\right],
0\displaystyle 0 =v0n+1​(u0n+1+λ​p0n+1),\displaystyle=v_{0}^{n+1}\left(u_{0}^{n+1}+\lambda p_{0}^{n+1}\right),

which leads that R−1n+1=0R_{-1}^{n+1}=0. Next comparing O⁡(ϵ0)O(\epsilon^{0}) term in the left and right sides of the scheme, for given τ\tau, we have

p0n+1−p0nτ\displaystyle\frac{p_{0}^{n+1}-p_{0}^{n}}{\tau} =u1n+∑i+j=1(−λ​uin​pjn+1−λ​vin​pjn+1),\displaystyle=u_{1}^{n}+\sum_{i+j=1}\left(-\lambda u_{i}^{n}p_{j}^{n+1}-\lambda v_{i}^{n}p_{j}^{n+1}\right),
u0n+1−u0nτ−d1​Δ​u0n+1\displaystyle\frac{u_{0}^{n+1}-u_{0}^{n}}{\tau}-d_{1}\Delta u_{0}^{n+1} =−λ​u1n+1+∑i+j=1(−uin+1​vjn+λ​uin+1​pjn+1),\displaystyle=-\lambda u_{1}^{n+1}+\sum_{i+j=1}\left(-u_{i}^{n+1}v_{j}^{n}+\lambda u_{i}^{n+1}p_{j}^{n+1}\right),
v0n+1−v0nτ−d2​Δ​v0n+1\displaystyle\frac{v_{0}^{n+1}-v_{0}^{n}}{\tau}-d_{2}\Delta v_{0}^{n+1} =∑i+j=1(uin+1​vjn+1+λ​vin+1​pjn+1).\displaystyle=\sum_{i+j=1}\left(u_{i}^{n+1}v_{j}^{n+1}+\lambda v_{i}^{n+1}p_{j}^{n+1}\right).

Thus

R0n+1=(u0n+1−v0n+1+λ​p0n+1)−(u0n−v0n+λ​p0n)τ−d1​Δ​u0n+1+d2​Δ​v0n+1.\displaystyle R_{0}^{n+1}=\frac{\left(u_{0}^{n+1}-v_{0}^{n+1}+\lambda p_{0}^{n+1}\right)-\left(u_{0}^{n}-v_{0}^{n}+\lambda p_{0}^{n}\right)}{\tau}-d_{1}\Delta u_{0}^{n+1}+d_{2}\Delta v_{0}^{n+1}.

R0n+1\displaystyle R_{0}^{n+1} =(un+1−vn+1+λ​pn+1)−(un−vn+λ​pn)τ−d1​Δ​un+1+d2​Δ​vn+1+O⁡(ϵτ)+O⁡(ϵ)\displaystyle=\frac{\left(u^{n+1}-v^{n+1}+\lambda p^{n+1}\right)-\left(u^{n}-v^{n}+\lambda p^{n}\right)}{\tau}-d_{1}\Delta u^{n+1}+d_{2}\Delta v^{n+1}+O(\frac{\epsilon}{\tau})+O(\epsilon)
=∂tw⁡(x,tn+1)−d1​Δ​u​(x,tn+1)+d2​Δ​v​(x,tn+1)+O⁡(τ)+O⁡(ϵτ)+O⁡(ϵ)\displaystyle=\partial_{t}w(x,t_{n+1})-d_{1}\Delta u(x,t_{n+1})+d_{2}\Delta v(x,t_{n+1})+O(\tau)+O(\frac{\epsilon}{\tau})+O(\epsilon)
=O⁡(τ),ϵ→0.\displaystyle=O(\tau),~~\epsilon\to 0.

Let the temporal size τ\tau tends to 0, then R0n+1R_{0}^{n+1} tends to 0, that is to say, the semi-discrete solution wn=un−vn+λ​pnw^{n}=u^{n}-v^{n}+\lambda p^{n} is a good approximation to the solution of the Stefan problem (9) as long as ϵ\epsilon tends to 0 and τ\tau is small enough.

2.2 First-order fully discrete semi-implicit scheme

Now following the semi-implicit treatment in Subsection 2.1, we introduce the fully discrete semi-implicit scheme of the system (1)-(3) equipped with the initial condition (4) and Dirichlet boundary conditions

γ(x,t)=γ∂Ω(t),γ=u,v,x=(x1,⋯,xd)′∈∂Ω,t>0,\displaystyle\gamma(x,t)=\gamma_{\partial\Omega}(t),~~\gamma=u,v,~~x=(x_{1},\cdots,x_{d})^{\prime}\in\partial\Omega,~~t>0, (49)

where γ∂Ω​(t)\gamma_{\partial\Omega}(t) for γ=u,v\gamma=u,v is some given function and the computational domain Ω=[a,b]d,b>a,\Omega=[a,b]^{d},b>a, is considered for simplicity. If given the number of the spatial grid nodes NN, the uniform mesh grid on Ω×[0,T]\Omega\times[0,T] with the spatial size h=(b−a)/Nh=(b-a)/N and the temporal size τ\tau is given as 𝒯τ,h={(x𝒋,tn)|𝒋=(j1,⋯,jd)′,x𝒋=(x1j1,⋯,xdjd)′,xiji=a+jih,tn=nτ,h=(b−a)/N,ji=0,1,⋯,N,n=1,2,⋯,i=1,⋯,d}\mathcal{T}_{\tau,h}=\{(x_{\bm{j}},t_{n})~\big|~\bm{j}=(j_{1},\cdots,j_{d})^{\prime},~x_{\bm{j}}=({x_{1}}_{j_{1}},\cdots,{x_{d}}_{j_{d}})^{\prime},~{x_{i}}_{j_{i}}=a+j_{i}h,~t_{n}=n\tau,~h=(b-a)/N,~j_{i}=0,1,\cdots,N,~n=1,2,\cdots,~i=1,\cdots,d\}. For any 𝒋\bm{j} in the interior and n=1,2,⋯n=1,2,\cdots, a fully discrete semi-implicit scheme of the equations (1)-(3) reads as

p𝒋n+1−p𝒋nτ\displaystyle\frac{p_{\bm{j}}^{n+1}-p_{\bm{j}}^{n}}{\tau} =1ϵ​[(1−p𝒋n+1)​u𝒋n−v𝒋n​p𝒋n+1],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\epsilon}[(1-p_{\bm{j}}^{n+1})u_{\bm{j}}^{n}-v_{\bm{j}}^{n}p_{\bm{j}}^{n+1}], (50)
u𝒋n+1−u𝒋nτ−d1​Δh​u𝒋n+1\displaystyle\frac{u_{\bm{j}}^{n+1}-u_{\bm{j}}^{n}}{\tau}-d_{1}\Delta_{h}u_{\bm{j}}^{n+1} =−1ϵ​u𝒋n+1​[v𝒋n+λ⁡(1−p𝒋n+1)],\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}u_{\bm{j}}^{n+1}[v_{\bm{j}}^{n}+\lambda(1-p_{\bm{j}}^{n+1})], (51)
v𝒋n+1−v𝒋nτ−d2​Δh​v𝒋n+1\displaystyle\frac{v_{\bm{j}}^{n+1}-v_{\bm{j}}^{n}}{\tau}-d_{2}\Delta_{h}v_{\bm{j}}^{n+1} =−1ϵ​v𝒋n+1​(u𝒋n+1+λ​p𝒋n+1),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}v_{\bm{j}}^{n+1}(u_{\bm{j}}^{n+1}+\lambda p_{\bm{j}}^{n+1}), (52)

where p𝒋n,u𝒋np_{\bm{j}}^{n},u_{\bm{j}}^{n} and v𝒋nv_{\bm{j}}^{n} are the finite difference solutions on the node (x𝒋,tn)(x_{\bm{j}},t_{n}), Δh\Delta_{h} is the second-order center difference operator. In the initial time steps, for x𝒋∈Ωx_{\bm{j}}\in\Omega, we choose

p𝒋0=p⁡(x𝒋,0),u𝒋0=u⁡(x𝒋,0),v𝒋0=v⁡(x𝒋,0).\displaystyle p_{\bm{j}}^{0}=p(x_{\bm{j}},0),\quad u_{\bm{j}}^{0}=u(x_{\bm{j}},0),\quad v_{\bm{j}}^{0}=v(x_{\bm{j}},0). (53)

And the discrete Dirichlet boundary conditions are given as

u⁡(x𝒋,tn)=u∂Ω​(tn),v⁡(x𝒋,tn)=v∂Ω​(tn),\displaystyle u(x_{\bm{j}},t_{n})=u_{\partial\Omega}(t_{n}),\quad v(x_{\bm{j}},t_{n})=v_{\partial\Omega}(t_{n}), (54)

where x𝒋∈∂Ωx_{\bm{j}}\in\partial\Omega, i.e. ∃i=1,⋯,d\exists\ i=1,\cdots,d, such that ji=0j_{i}=0 or NN. Rewrite the schemes (50)-(52) as the following form, for any 𝒋\bm{j} and n=1,2,⋯n=1,2,\cdots,

[1+τϵ​(u𝒋n+v𝒋n)]​p𝒋n+1\displaystyle\left[1+\frac{\tau}{\epsilon}(u_{\bm{j}}^{n}+v_{\bm{j}}^{n})\right]p_{\bm{j}}^{n+1} =p𝒋n+τϵ​u𝒋n,\displaystyle=p_{\bm{j}}^{n}+\frac{\tau}{\epsilon}u_{\bm{j}}^{n}, (55)
[1+τϵ​(v𝒋n+λ⁡(1−p𝒋n+1))−d1​τ​Δh]​u𝒋n+1\displaystyle\left[1+\frac{\tau}{\epsilon}(v_{\bm{j}}^{n}+\lambda(1-p_{\bm{j}}^{n+1}))-d_{1}\tau\Delta_{h}\right]u_{\bm{j}}^{n+1} =u𝒋n,\displaystyle=u_{\bm{j}}^{n}, (56)
[1+τϵ​(u𝒋n+1+λ​p𝒋n+1)−d2​τ​Δh]​v𝒋n+1\displaystyle\left[1+\frac{\tau}{\epsilon}(u_{\bm{j}}^{n+1}+\lambda p_{\bm{j}}^{n+1})-d_{2}\tau\Delta_{h}\right]v_{\bm{j}}^{n+1} =v𝒋n,\displaystyle=v_{\bm{j}}^{n}, (57)

where Δh\Delta_{h} is the three- and five-point center difference operator for one- and two-dimensional case respectively. Take d=1d=1 as an example, then the first-order fully discrete semi-implicit scheme (55)-(57) in one-dimension becomes

[1+τϵ​(ujn+vjn)]​pjn+1\displaystyle\left[1+\frac{\tau}{\epsilon}(u_{j}^{n}+v_{j}^{n})\right]p_{j}^{n+1} =pjn+τϵ​ujn,\displaystyle=p_{j}^{n}+\frac{\tau}{\epsilon}u_{j}^{n}, (58)
[1+τϵ​(vjn+λ⁡(1−pjn+1))+2​d1​τh2]​ujn+1−d1​τh2​uj+1n+1−d1​τh2​uj−1n+1\displaystyle\left[1+\frac{\tau}{\epsilon}(v_{j}^{n}+\lambda(1-p_{j}^{n+1}))+2d_{1}\frac{\tau}{h^{2}}\right]u_{j}^{n+1}-d_{1}\frac{\tau}{h^{2}}u_{j+1}^{n+1}-d_{1}\frac{\tau}{h^{2}}u_{j-1}^{n+1} =ujn,\displaystyle=u_{j}^{n}, (59)
[1+τϵ​(ujn+1+λ​pjn+1)+2​d2​τh2]​vjn+1−d2​τh2​vj+1n+1−d2​τh2​vj−1n+1\displaystyle\left[1+\frac{\tau}{\epsilon}(u_{j}^{n+1}+\lambda p_{j}^{n+1})+2d_{2}\frac{\tau}{h^{2}}\right]v_{j}^{n+1}-d_{2}\frac{\tau}{h^{2}}v_{j+1}^{n+1}-d_{2}\frac{\tau}{h^{2}}v_{j-1}^{n+1} =vjn.\displaystyle=v_{j}^{n}. (60)

Next, we show that like the semi-discrete scheme (13)-(15), the first-order fully discrete semi-implicit scheme (55)-(57) combined with the discrete initial condition (53) and boundary conditions (54) preserves various properties of the system (1)-(3), including the non-negativity preserving property, L2L^{2} estimate, and the stability result for the corresponding linearized version.

Theorem 2.1 (Bound preserving).

Consider the first-order semi-implicit scheme (55)-(57). Assume that the discrete initial condition 0≤u𝐣0≤Cu0\leq u_{\bm{j}}^{0}\leq C_{u}, 0≤v𝐣0≤Cv0\leq v_{\bm{j}}^{0}\leq C_{v} and 0≤p𝐣0⩽10\leq p_{\bm{j}}^{0}\leqslant 1 for all 𝐣{\bm{j}}, the discrete Dirichlet boundary condition 0≤u∂Ω​(tn)≤Cu0\leq u_{\partial\Omega}(t_{n})\leq C_{u}, 0≤v∂Ω​(tn)≤Cv0\leq v_{\partial\Omega}(t_{n})\leq C_{v} for n=1,2,⋯n=1,2,\cdots, then one has 0≤u𝐣n≤Cu0\leq u_{\bm{j}}^{n}\leq C_{u}, 0≤v𝐣n≤Cv0\leq v_{\bm{j}}^{n}\leq C_{v} and 0≤p𝐣n⩽10\leq p_{\bm{j}}^{n}\leqslant 1 for all 𝐣\bm{j}.

Proof.

(61)

3 High order semi-implicit Runge–Kutta scheme

In this part, we consider a high order semi-implicit Runge–Kutta scheme which is used in the case that the stiff terms don’t appear in partitioned or additive form and the stiffness is associated to some variables [3]. In order to apply this idea, we rewrite the stiff system (1)-(3) as

∂tu−d1​Δ​u¯\displaystyle\partial_{t}u-d_{1}\Delta\overline{u} =−1ϵ​u¯​[v+λ⁡(1−p)],x∈ℝd,t>0,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}\overline{u}\left[v+\lambda\left(1-p\right)\right],~~x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},~~t>0, (63)
∂tv−d2​Δ​v¯\displaystyle\partial_{t}v-d_{2}\Delta\overline{v} =−1ϵ​v¯​(u+λ​p),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}\overline{v}\left(u+\lambda p\right), (64)
∂tp\displaystyle\partial_{t}p =1ϵ​(u¯−u​p¯−v​p¯),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(\overline{u}-u\overline{p}-v\overline{p}\right), (65)

where u¯=u\overline{u}=u, v¯=v\overline{v}=v and p¯=p\overline{p}=p. Define the vector y=(u,v,p)′y=(u,v,p)^{\prime} and z=(u¯,v¯,p¯)′z=(\overline{u},\overline{v},\overline{p})^{\prime}, then the equations (63)-(65) can be written in the following form,

∂ty\displaystyle\partial_{t}y =ℋ⁡(y,z),\displaystyle=\mathcal{H}(y,z),
∂tz\displaystyle\partial_{t}z =ℋ⁡(y,z),\displaystyle=\mathcal{H}(y,z),

with the right hand side

ℋ⁡(y,z):=[d1​Δ​u¯−1ϵ​u¯​[v+λ⁡(1−p)]d2​Δ​v¯​(t)−1ϵ​v¯​(u+λ​p)1ϵ​(u¯−u​p¯−v​p¯)].\displaystyle\mathcal{H}(y,z):=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}d_{1}\Delta\overline{u}-\frac{1}{\epsilon}\overline{u}\left[v+\lambda(1-p)\right]\\ d_{2}\Delta\overline{v}(t)-\frac{1}{\epsilon}\overline{v}(u+\lambda p)\\ \frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(\overline{u}-u\overline{p}-v\overline{p}\right)\\ \end{array}\right].

The diffusion term is treated implicitly as it induces some stiffness, and zz is treated implicitly while yy is treated explicitly. Set zn=ynz^{n}=y^{n} and compute the stage fluxes for i=1,⋯,si=1,\cdots,s,

Yi\displaystyle Y_{i} =yn+τ∑j=1i−1a^i​jkj,i=2,⋯,s,\displaystyle=y^{n}+\tau\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\hat{a}_{ij}k_{j},~~i=2,\cdots,s, (69)
Z~i\displaystyle\tilde{Z}_{i} =yn+τ∑j=1i−1ai​jkj,i=2,⋯,s,\displaystyle=y^{n}+\tau\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}a_{ij}k_{j},~~i=2,\cdots,s, (70)
ki\displaystyle k_{i} =ℋ(Yi,Z~i+τai​iki),i=1,⋯,s,\displaystyle=\mathcal{H}\left(Y_{i},\tilde{Z}_{i}+\tau a_{ii}k_{i}\right),~~i=1,\cdots,s, (71)

with Y1=Z~1=ynY_{1}=\tilde{Z}_{1}=y^{n}. Then the solution yn+1=yn+τ​∑i=1sb^i​kiy^{n+1}=y^{n}+\tau\sum_{i=1}^{s}\hat{b}_{i}k_{i}. Hence combined with proper discretization in space, an high order semi-implicit Runge–Kutta scheme is proposed.

In this part, we adopt the 2-stage second-order semi-implicit Runge–Kutta scheme whose double Butcher tableau is

We mention again that such a semi-implicit Runge–Kutta scheme in Section 3 is practically of second-order accuracy in both time and space and numerical tests on the convergence order in time will be carried out in next Section.

4 Numerical tests

In this section, we provide various numerical tests to verify the accuracy of the first- and second-order schemes in Section 2 and Section 3. Besides the order of accuracy, we also observe the non-negativity and bound preserving property, and the capture of the sharp interface with various ϵ\epsilon on the numerical side. At last we simulate the dynamics of the substances and the substrate, the liquid solidification process, etc.

4.1 Convergence tests

The errors of numerical solutions {γ𝒋n}\{\gamma^{n}_{\bm{j}}\} for γ=u,v,p,w\gamma=u,v,p,w are computed as follows,

eγτ,h∞:=max𝒋⁡|γ𝒋n−γref​(𝒙𝒋,tn)|,\displaystyle{e_{\gamma}}_{\tau,h}^{\infty}:=\max_{\bm{j}}|\gamma^{n}_{\bm{j}}-\gamma^{\text{ref}}(\bm{x}_{\bm{j}},t_{n})|,
eγτ,h1:=h​∑𝒋|γ𝒋n−γref​(𝒙𝒋,tn)|,\displaystyle{e_{\gamma}}_{\tau,h}^{1}:=h\sum_{\bm{j}}|\gamma^{n}_{\bm{j}}-\gamma^{\text{ref}}(\bm{x}_{\bm{j}},t_{n})|,
eγτ,h2:=[h​∑𝒋|γ𝒋n−γref​(𝒙𝒋,tn)|2]12,\displaystyle{e_{\gamma}}_{\tau,h}^{2}:=\left[h\sum_{\bm{j}}|\gamma^{n}_{\bm{j}}-\gamma^{\text{ref}}(\bm{x}_{\bm{j}},t_{n})|^{2}\right]^{\frac{1}{2}},

where j=(j1,⋯,jd)′j=(j_{1},\cdots,j_{d})^{\prime}, 𝒙𝒋=(x1j1,⋯,xdjd)′\bm{x}_{\bm{j}}=({x_{1}}_{j_{1}},\cdots,{x_{d}}_{j_{d}})^{\prime}, hh is the spatial mesh size, τ\tau is the temporal mesh size, and γref\gamma^{\text{ref}} is the reference solution which is obtained by small enough hh and τ\tau.

4.1.1 Convergence test for the first-order semi-implicit scheme

Case 1: a one-dimensional test with ϵ∼O⁡(1)\epsilon\sim O(1). Consider the fast reaction–diffusion system (1)-(3). 4.2 Limit behavior

4.2.1 One-dimensional case

In order to demonstrate the limit behavior of the fast reaction–diffusion system (1)-(3), we consider the following model with Dirichlet boundary conditions on the domain [−L,L]×[0,T][-L,L]\times[0,T],

∂tuϵ−d1​Δ​uϵ=−1ϵ​uϵ​[vϵ+λ⁡(1−pϵ)],\displaystyle\partial_{t}u_{\epsilon}-d_{1}\Delta u_{\epsilon}=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}u_{\epsilon}[v_{\epsilon}+\lambda(1-p_{\epsilon})], (96)
∂tvϵ−d2​Δ​vϵ=−1ϵ​vϵ​(uϵ+λ​pϵ),\displaystyle\partial_{t}v_{\epsilon}-d_{2}\Delta v_{\epsilon}=-\frac{1}{\epsilon}v_{\epsilon}(u_{\epsilon}+\lambda p_{\epsilon}),
∂tpϵ=1ϵ​[(1−pϵ)​uϵ−vϵ​pϵ],\displaystyle\partial_{t}p_{\epsilon}=\frac{1}{\epsilon}[(1-p_{\epsilon})u_{\epsilon}-v_{\epsilon}p_{\epsilon}],
uϵ(x,0)=θd1,vϵ(x,0)=0,pϵ(x,0)=1,\displaystyle u_{\epsilon}(x,0)=\frac{\theta}{d_{1}},\quad v_{\epsilon}(x,0)=0,\quad p_{\epsilon}(x,0)=1,
uϵ(−L,t)=0,vϵ(−L,t)=Std2,pϵ(−L,t)=0,\displaystyle u_{\epsilon}(-L,t)=0,\quad v_{\epsilon}(-L,t)=\frac{S_{t}}{d_{2}},\quad p_{\epsilon}(-L,t)=0,
uϵ(L,t)=θd1,vϵ(L,t)=0,pϵ(L,t)=1,\displaystyle u_{\epsilon}(L,t)=\frac{\theta}{d_{1}},\quad v_{\epsilon}(L,t)=0,\quad p_{\epsilon}(L,t)=1,

where d1=1d_{1}=1, d2=2d_{2}=2, λ=1\lambda=1, θ=0.05\theta=0.05, St=0.25S_{t}=0.25, L=1L=1, T=1T=1.

In this test, we first investigate the dynamic behavior of the solutions to the system (96). We first take ϵ=10−2\epsilon=10^{-2} and the mesh size h=0.0125h=0.0125 and τ=5×10−6\tau=5\times 10^{-6}. Figure 3 shows the results of u,v,pu,v,p and the enthalpy function ww at time tt from 00 to 11. We can numerically check the positivity and bound preserving properties, which agrees with the numerical analysis in Section 2. Furthermore, as the strength of the reaction is much greater than that of the diffusion process, we can find that the increase or decrease of uu is consistent with pp, and the opposite is true for vv. Next we retake ϵ=10−4\epsilon=10^{-4}, Figure 4 shows the corresponding results with h=6.25×10−3h=6.25\times 10^{-3} and τ=5×10−6\tau=5\times 10^{-6}. After comparing the dynamic behavior of the solutions with different ϵ\epsilon, we can conclude that the smaller the ϵ\epsilon the sharper the interface. The sharp interface is referred to as the phase transition interface in the limit Stefan problem, whose speed is determined by the Stefan’s condition. In this way, assume that the system is full of liquid at the initial moment, such as water, and give a freezing stimulus at the left edge of the system, then we can conclude that the liquid exothermizes and freezes, and the movement of the sharp interface moving to the right inscribes the liquid solidification process. Then Figure 5 shows more details on the sharp interface with various ϵ\epsilon.

From Figure 6 we can conclude that for the first-order scheme, smaller parameters ϵ\epsilon impose tighter requirements on the mesh size. Combined with the limit behavior, proposing an asymptotic preserving scheme on ϵ\epsilon, which avoids the use of very fine meshes, is our future consideration.

Figure 7 and 8 give the results of the enthalpy function ww and the temperature θ=B⁡(w)\theta=B(w) of the substance with ϵ=10−5\epsilon=10^{-5} and the mesh size Δ​x=0.05\Delta x=0.05, τ=0.001\tau=0.001.

5 Conclusions

In this paper, we study the semi-implicit strategy on the fast reaction–diffusion equations (1)-(4) and develop the semi-implicit schemes with first- and second-order accurate in time respectively. And our semi-implicit scheme preserves some analytical properties of the original model at the semi- and fully-discrete level. We also provide a series of numerical tests to demonstrate the properties, such as numerical convergence, non-negativity, and bound preserving, and to capture the movement of the sharp interface with various ϵ\epsilon and to explore the heat transfer process, such as solid melting or liquid solidification.
